newsitem.title: USA: Dollar finishes firmer in U.S. as rumors swirl.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finishes firmer in U.S. as rumors swirl.

text.p: The dollar closed higher against the yen bolstered by talk that U.S. officials could tolerate a stronger domestic currency and by expectations for continued low Japanese interest rates, currency experts said.

Rumor swirled that Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the international finance bureau of Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF), said U.S. officials told him they could tolerate the dollar at an exchange rate of 120 yen, they said.
However, a source close to the MOF in New York said: "We have had no information about that. So, strictly speaking, we can't confirm and we can't deny..."
Shortly after the rumor surfaced, the dollar hit 111.70 yen, its high for the day.
Nevertheless, some currency traders doubted Sakakibara had made that remark.

"There's definitely yen selling because of this rumor...," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd. But he added: "I think it's just a rumor. He would never say something like that."
The dollar closed at 111.57/62 yen and 1.5292/97 marks, up from 111.12/22 yen and 1.5255/60 marks at the open.
Private sector machinery orders in Japan, excluding orders for ships and machinery at electric power firms, tumbled 11.1 percent in August after rising sharply in July.
The Bank of Japan has kept interest rates at record lows to help boost economic growth. The decline in machinery orders indicated the central bank will likely keep rates low.
"I think it means that there is less likelihood of an imminent rate hike," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. "It helps the dollar a little bit against the yen."

Bundesbank officials continued to emphasize on Tuesday that strict adherence to financial criteria is necessary for European countries to become members of the single currency planned for January 1999. Buba President Hans Tietmeyer stressed this point on Monday and his remarks were echoed by other officials on Tuesday, including Klaus-Dieter Kuebacher, president of the regional central bank in Berlin.

"They don't want to see window dressing and sort of fictitious accounting from countries who want to participate in the first round of monetary union," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Gilmore said the remarks suggest central bank officials could "argue for and perhaps achieve a delay in monetary union."
The German currency strengthened against some other European currencies and the dollar, but profit-taking later eroded its gains, traders said.
The dollar as well as the French franc and Italian lira closed firmer against the mark.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.2535/45 Swiss francs, up from 1.2480/85 at the open.
Sterling ended at $1.5630/40, higher than $1.5610/20 at the opening.
The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3536/41, down from C$1.3544/49.
The Australian dollar finished at $0.7908/13, up from $0.7878/83 at the opening.
-- Donna Sells 212 859 1668
